introduction: This intermediate tier explores the most heavily tested area of the SRA: the radical 2018 Amendments to Section 10, the contracts that CANNOT be specifically enforced, and the mechanics of Preventive Relief (Injunctions).

core_concepts.title: Section 10: The 2018 Paradigm Shift
core_concepts.description:
This is the most important exam update!
- Pre-2018: Specific performance was 'Discretionary'. The court *could* order it if damages were inadequate.
- Post-2018 Amendment: Specific performance is now **Mandatory**. Section 10 now states that the court **SHALL** enforce specific performance of a contract, subject only to exceptions in Sections 11(2), 14, and 16. It is no longer an exception; it is the rule.

core_concepts.title: Contracts NOT Specifically Enforceable (Section 14)
core_concepts.description:
Even post-2018, courts will NOT enforce specific performance for:
1. Substituted Performance: If the plaintiff has already got the contract performed by a third party (Sec 20).
2. Continuous Duty: Contracts requiring continuous court supervision (e.g., managing a complex business).
3. Personal Qualifications: Contracts dependent on the personal volition/skills of the parties (e.g., forcing a singer to sing, or a painter to paint). You cannot force artistic performance.
4. Determinable Contracts: Contracts that are in their nature determinable (can be terminated easily by either party).

core_concepts.title: Preventive Relief: Injunctions (Sections 36 to 42)
core_concepts.description:
An injunction is a court order restraining a person from doing a specific act, or requiring them to do a specific act.
- Temporary Injunctions: Granted at any stage of a suit to preserve the status quo until the final judgment. Governed by the Civil Procedure Code (CPC, Order 39), NOT the SRA.
- Perpetual (Permanent) Injunctions (Sec 38): Granted only at the final hearing/decree. It permanently stops the defendant from asserting a right or committing an act that violates the plaintiff's rights. Governed by the SRA.

core_concepts.title: Mandatory Injunctions (Section 39)
core_concepts.description: While normal injunctions stop you from doing something (negative), a Mandatory Injunction compels you to undo an unlawful act (positive) to prevent a breach of an obligation. (e.g., Ordering a neighbor to demolish a wall they built illegally on your property).

important_entities.name: Substituted Performance (Section 20)
important_entities.significance: If a party breaks a contract, the aggrieved party can now give a 30-day notice, get the work done by a *third party* (or by themselves), and then recover the costs/expenses from the defaulting party. However, once you choose substituted performance, you forfeit the right to demand specific performance.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'Under which section of the Specific Relief Act are Temporary Injunctions granted?' The answer is **NONE**. Section 37 explicitly states that temporary injunctions are regulated by the **Code of Civil Procedure (CPC)**. The SRA only regulates Perpetual and Mandatory injunctions.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: S C P D (Substituted, Continuous, Personal, Determinable)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember SCPD to quickly recall the four types of contracts a court will outright refuse to enforce under Section 14.

exam_strategy_tips: If a CLAT PG or Judiciary question asks 'Is specific performance of a contract a discretionary power of the court after 2018?', the answer is **NO**. The word 'may' was replaced with 'shall', making it a statutory right of the plaintiff.
